questions.question: A list can be looped over, yet it is not an iterator. Why not?
options: Because a list is mutable, and an iterator is required to be immutable.
Because a list holds every item at once, breaking the one-at-a-time rule.
Because a list has no `__iter__` method of its own to provide an iterator.
Because only the built-in sequence types are ever allowed to be iterators.
questions.explanation: Being loopable makes something iterable, but an iterator is specifically the object that produces items one at a time without materialising the whole sequence. A list has already materialised everything, so it supplies an iterator on request rather than being one. Every iterator is iterable, while the reverse does not hold.
questions.misconception: Iterable and iterator are not synonyms; one can be looped over, the other does the producing.

questions.question: A list of 100,000 numbers occupies roughly 800,000 bytes, while a range over the same span occupies about 48 bytes. What happens to each if the span grows to ten million?
options: Both grow by the same factor, since each now represents far more numbers.
The list stays flat while the range grows, as it tracks more positions.
Both stay completely flat, because Python compresses large sequences.
The list grows roughly a hundredfold, while the range stays near 48 bytes.
questions.explanation: The list stores every value, so its footprint scales with the count. The range computes each value as it is requested and keeps only its bounds and position, so its size is independent of the span. This is why looping over ten million numbers is unremarkable, and it is the same principle as reading a file in chunks: process one item, release it, move on.
questions.misconception: An iterator's memory does not grow with the number of items it can produce.

questions.question: How can you tell from an object's methods whether it is iterable, an iterator, or neither?
options: An iterable has `__next__`, while an iterator instead has `__iter__`.
An iterable has `__iter__`; an iterator has `__iter__` and `__next__`.
Both of them must have a `__loop__` method, differing in its return value.
Only an iterator has any special methods at all, and an iterable has none.
questions.explanation: The presence of the iteration method makes something loopable, and adding the advance method makes it an iterator capable of producing the next value on demand. That is also why an iterator satisfies both roles. A quick behavioural check works too: looping over an integer fails precisely because it has no iteration method.
questions.misconception: The advance method is what distinguishes an iterator; the iteration method alone only makes something iterable.

questions.question: What does a `for` loop actually do under the hood?
options: It indexes the object from zero upward until an IndexError is raised.
It copies the object into a list first, then walks that copy by position.
It gets an iterator once, then calls advance until StopIteration.
It counts the object's length and then loops exactly that many times.
questions.explanation: There is no hidden counter. The loop obtains an iterator, pulls one value at a time, and treats the stop signal as its termination condition, catching it silently. This is why a `for` loop works identically over a list, a set, a dictionary, or a generator, none of which are indexed the same way, and why you can rebuild the loop yourself with a while loop and a handler.
questions.misconception: A `for` loop is not index-based, which is why it works on unordered and lazily produced collections.

questions.question: What does calling the advance function on an exhausted iterator do, and how does a loop use that?
options: It raises StopIteration, which a `for` loop catches to end normally.
It returns `None`, which the surrounding loop then explicitly tests for.
It quietly restarts the iterator from the very beginning of its sequence.
It returns an empty value, exactly matching how a file read signals its end.
questions.explanation: The stop signal is an exception rather than a sentinel value, which means no legitimate data value can ever be mistaken for the end. The loop catches it quietly, so you never see it unless you drive the iterator yourself. This differs from file reading, where an empty string is the agreed end marker.
questions.misconception: Exhaustion raises rather than returning a special value, and nothing restarts automatically.

questions.question: What is the essential behavioural difference between `return` and `yield`?
options: `yield` returns several values at once, whereas `return` returns only one.
`yield` is faster than `return` because it skips the function call overhead.
`yield` may appear only once in a function, while `return` can appear often.
`return` ends the function and discards state; `yield` pauses and keeps it.
questions.explanation: A normal function runs to completion and is gone. A generator suspends itself at each yield, keeping everything it had, and continues from exactly there when the next value is requested. That pause-and-remember behaviour is the whole mechanism: it lets a function hand out values one at a time over its lifetime instead of computing them all and returning a collection.
questions.misconception: A generator does not produce all its values at once; it produces one and suspends.

questions.question: What happens the moment you call a generator function?
options: Its body runs forward to the first yield, and that first value is returned.
Nothing in the body runs; it returns a generator object you then drive.
Its entire body runs and the yielded values are collected into a list.
An error is raised at once unless the call happens to be inside a loop.
questions.explanation: Calling it only builds the generator object. No statement in the body executes until the first value is requested, at which point the body runs up to the first yield and suspends. This laziness is why a generator over an expensive or infinite computation costs nothing to create.
questions.misconception: Creating a generator does no work; requesting a value is what runs the body.

questions.scenario: A script assigns a generator to a name, loops over it and prints every value successfully, then loops over the same name again to compute a total. The second loop produces nothing and the total is zero.
questions.question: Why is the second pass empty?
options: The first loop deleted the generator object from memory once it finished.
A generator must be converted with the iteration function before reuse.
A generator holds its position, so once exhausted it stays exhausted.
The total is zero because a generator yields only to the first consumer.
questions.explanation: The single generator object carries the state of where it has got to, and reaching the end leaves it there permanently with no rewind. This is the trade for not storing the values: they are gone once consumed. Call the generator function again for a second independent pass, or materialise the values into a list if you genuinely need to traverse them more than once.
questions.misconception: A generator is single-use; it is not a reusable collection.

questions.question: What is the difference between a list comprehension and a generator expression?
options: Square brackets build the whole list now; round brackets produce on demand.
They are completely identical, and the two bracket styles are interchangeable.
Round brackets build a tuple, which is just an immutable version of a list.
A generator expression is only allowed to be written inside a function body.
questions.explanation: The syntax differs by one character and the consequence is substantial: one materialises every value immediately, the other holds almost nothing and computes each value when asked. For a large span, the generator form avoids building a collection you only intend to walk once. Round brackets do produce a tuple when used around a literal sequence, but with a `for` clause inside they produce a generator.
questions.misconception: The bracket style determines whether the values are computed now or later.

questions.question: A generator contains a `while True` loop that yields an ever-increasing number. Why is this safe?
options: Because Python silently caps every generator at a fixed number of values.
Because only the current value is held, so the stream can be unbounded.
Because the endless loop will eventually raise StopIteration on its own.
It is not safe at all and will exhaust memory the moment it is first called.
questions.explanation: Suspension after each yield means the generator never gets ahead of its consumer, so an endless sequence costs no more than a single value. Nothing is produced until requested, and the consumer ends the process by stopping or breaking. Modelling a stream with no natural end is one of the capabilities a plain list cannot offer at all.
questions.misconception: An infinite generator is harmless because it is lazy; the danger would be collecting its output into a list.

questions.question: Why are generators central to processing large image datasets for deep learning?
options: They compress each image on the way in so the whole dataset fits in memory.
They speed training up by quietly skipping the slowest samples in the set.
A folder far larger than memory can be streamed one item or batch at a time.
They convert images to arrays more accurately than loading them all at once.
questions.explanation: A twenty gigabyte folder cannot sit in eight gigabytes of memory, so the practical pattern is a generator that opens one image, converts it, yields it, and moves on. Library batch generators are precisely this idea packaged up. The benefit is capacity rather than speed or accuracy: it makes datasets of arbitrary size workable on ordinary hardware.
questions.misconception: Streaming addresses the memory ceiling, not training speed.

questions.question: Calling the iteration function on an object that is already an iterator returns the same object rather than a new one. Why does that matter?
options: It makes the iterator reusable, since its position resets on each such call.
It means that an iterator cannot be used directly inside a `for` loop at all.
It allows two separate loops to consume the one iterator independently.
It is why an iterator is also iterable, so a `for` loop consumes it directly.
questions.explanation: Because its iteration method hands back itself, an iterator satisfies the requirement a `for` loop places on whatever it is given, which is what lets you loop over a generator with no conversion step. It also explains why two loops over the same iterator share one position rather than proceeding independently, so the second sees only what the first left behind.
questions.misconception: Returning itself means the position is shared, which is the opposite of resetting.

questions.question: Explain the mechanism that lets a generator produce values lazily, and why writing one is so much lighter than writing a custom iterator by hand.
questions.answer: A generator suspends at each yield rather than finishing, retaining its local variables and its exact position, and resumes from that point when the next value is requested. Because the function itself carries the state between requests, the values are produced one at a time and only on demand. Writing the equivalent by hand means an iterable class whose iteration method returns a separate iterator class, which must implement both the iteration method returning itself and the advance method producing values or signalling the end, so a two-line generator function replaces two classes and three protocol methods.
questions.explanation: That is the trade generators make explicit: the language takes over the bookkeeping of position and state that the manual protocol forces you to write out, while the observable behaviour is identical.

questions.question: Define iteration, iterable, and iterator, and state the relationship between the last two.
questions.answer: Iteration is the process of taking each item of a collection one after another, which is what any loop over a group of items performs. An iterable is an object you can loop over, such as a list, tuple, set, dictionary, or string. An iterator is the object that actually drives the iteration, producing one item at a time without holding the whole sequence. The relationship is one-directional: every iterator is also iterable, but not every iterable is an iterator, because something like a list has all its items in memory already.
questions.explanation: Keeping the three apart is what makes the rest comprehensible, since a `for` loop is simply iteration performed by requesting an iterator from an iterable and then pulling from it until it signals that it is finished.
